blocks.body:
An equation such as $x^2 = 4$ usually has a few solutions. An inequality such as $x^2 < 4$ usually has infinitely many, here every number strictly between $-2$ and $2$. Solving an inequality means describing that whole set exactly, usually as an interval or a union of intervals.

The algebra looks like equation solving, with two traps: multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality, and multiplying by an expression whose sign you do not know is not allowed at all. This page gives the rules, the sign-chart method that handles polynomial and rational inequalities, and the tricks for absolute values and square roots.

blocks.title: Notation and the basic rules
blocks.body:
Interval notation: $(a, b)$ is the set of $x$ with $a < x < b$; a square bracket includes the endpoint, so $[a, b)$ means $a \le x < b$; $(-\infty, b]$ means $x \le b$. The symbol $\cup$ joins sets: $(-\infty, -1) \cup (3, \infty)$ is "less than $-1$ or greater than 3".

Everything rests on one idea: $a < b$ means that $b - a$ is positive, and positive numbers are closed under addition and multiplication. From this:

1. If $a < b$, then $a + c < b + c$ for every $c$, because $(b + c) - (a + c) = b - a$.
2. If $a < b$ and $c > 0$, then $ac < bc$, because $bc - ac = (b - a)c$ is a product of positives.
3. If $a < b$ and $c < 0$, then $ac > bc$, because $ac - bc = (b - a)(-c)$ is a product of positives.
4. If $0 \le a < b$, then $a^2 < b^2$, because $b^2 - a^2 = (b - a)(b + a)$ with both factors positive. Squaring needs both sides non-negative: $-3 < 2$ but $9 > 4$.

Example: $-2x + 5 > 11$ gives $-2x > 6$, and dividing by $-2$ reverses the sign: $x < -3$. A compound inequality is handled in one go: $-3 < 2x + 1 \le 7$ gives $-4 < 2x \le 6$, so $-2 < x \le 3$, that is, $x \in (-2, 3]$.

blocks.title: Quadratic inequalities
blocks.body:
The graph of a quadratic tells you where it is positive (see [[quadratics]]). Take $x^2 - x - 6 = (x + 2)(x - 3)$. Its parabola opens upward and crosses the axis at $-2$ and $3$, so it is below the axis between the roots and above it outside. Hence

$$x^2 - x - 6 < 0 \iff -2 < x < 3, \qquad x^2 - x - 6 \ge 0 \iff x \le -2 \text{ or } x \ge 3.$$

A quick table confirms it: at $x = -3, 0, 4$ the values are $6, -6, 6$.

If the discriminant is negative the parabola never meets the axis, so the quadratic has the same sign as $a$ for every $x$. For example $x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4 > 0$ always, so $x^2 + 2x + 5 < 0$ has no solutions and $x^2 + 2x + 5 > 0$ holds for all real $x$.

blocks.title: Sign of a quadratic
blocks.body:
Let $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ with $a \ne 0$ and $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$.

1. If $\Delta > 0$ and the roots are $r < s$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $-a$ for $r < x < s$, and the sign of $a$ for $x < r$ and for $x > s$.
2. If $\Delta = 0$ with repeated root $r$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $a$ for every $x \ne r$.
3. If $\Delta < 0$, then $f(x)$ has the sign of $a$ for every real $x$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: In case 1, $f(x) = a(x - r)(x - s)$. For $r < x < s$ the factor $x - r$ is positive and $x - s$ is negative, so the product $(x-r)(x-s)$ is negative; outside $[r, s]$ both factors have the same sign, so it is positive. Multiplying by $a$ gives the claim. In case 2, $f(x) = a(x - r)^2$, and $(x - r)^2 > 0$ for $x \ne r$. In case 3, completing the square gives $f(x) = a\left[\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \frac{-\Delta}{4a^2}\right]$, and the bracket is positive since $-\Delta > 0$.

blocks.title: Sign charts for products and quotients
blocks.body:
The proof above generalises. A product of linear factors can only change sign where one of its factors is zero, so:

1. Move everything to one side, so the inequality compares a single expression with 0.
2. Factor it completely, numerator and denominator.
3. Mark the zeros of every factor on the number line. They split it into intervals.
4. On each interval, every factor has a constant sign; count the negative factors (or test one point) to find the sign of the whole expression.
5. Read off the intervals with the required sign. Include zeros of the numerator for $\le$ or $\ge$, and never include zeros of the denominator.

For $(x - 1)(x + 2)(x - 4) > 0$, the critical points are $-2, 1, 4$. For $x > 4$ all three factors are positive, and each time $x$ passes a critical point going left, exactly one factor changes sign. So the signs on $(-\infty, -2)$, $(-2, 1)$, $(1, 4)$, $(4, \infty)$ are $-, +, -, +$, and the solution is $(-2, 1) \cup (4, \infty)$.

A squared factor such as $(x - 3)^2$ does not change sign at $x = 3$; only factors raised to odd powers do.

For rational inequalities the crucial rule is: do not multiply both sides by a denominator unless you know its sign. Subtract instead and combine into one fraction, as in the next example. (One may also multiply by the square of the denominator, which is positive, but the fraction method is cleaner.)

blocks.title: A rational inequality
blocks.solution:
Multiplying by $x - 2$ would be wrong, since $x - 2$ is negative for $x < 2$. Instead,

$$\frac{x + 1}{x - 2} - 2 = \frac{x + 1 - 2(x - 2)}{x - 2} = \frac{5 - x}{x - 2} \le 0, \quad\text{equivalently}\quad \frac{x - 5}{x - 2} \ge 0.$$

Critical points: $x = 2$ (excluded, the expression is undefined) and $x = 5$ (included, the expression is 0). Signs of $\frac{x-5}{x-2}$ on $(-\infty, 2)$, $(2, 5)$, $(5, \infty)$: $+, -, +$. Solution: $(-\infty, 2) \cup [5, \infty)$.

Check: $x = 0$ gives $-\frac12 \le 2$, true; $x = 3$ gives $4 \le 2$, false; $x = 5$ gives $2 \le 2$, true; $x = 6$ gives $\frac74 \le 2$, true. Had we multiplied through by $x - 2$, we would have found $x \ge 5$ only and lost all of $(-\infty, 2)$.

blocks.title: Absolute values and square roots
blocks.body:
The absolute value $|x - a|$ is the distance between $x$ and $a$ on the number line. So for $d > 0$:

$$|x - a| < d \iff a - d < x < a + d, \qquad |x - a| > d \iff x < a - d \text{ or } x > a + d.$$

For example $|2x - 3| < 5$ means $-5 < 2x - 3 < 5$, so $-1 < x < 4$. When both sides involve $x$, or there are several absolute values, split into cases according to the sign of each expression inside.

With square roots, first find the domain (the expression under the root must be non-negative), and only square both sides when both are known to be non-negative, by rule 4. This usually means splitting into cases.

blocks.title: Absolute values
blocks.solution:
(a) An absolute value is never negative, so a solution needs $x + 1 \ge 0$, and then the inequality says $-(x + 1) \le 2x - 3 \le x + 1$. The left part gives $3x \ge 2$, so $x \ge \frac23$; the right part gives $x \le 4$. Both force $x + 1 > 0$ automatically. Solution: $\left[\frac23, 4\right]$. Check at the ends: at $x = \frac23$ both sides equal $\frac53$; at $x = 4$ both equal 5.

(b) The expressions inside change sign at $x = 1$ and $x = -2$.

- If $x < -2$: the sum is $(1 - x) + (-x - 2) = -2x - 1 < 5$, so $x > -3$. This gives $(-3, -2)$.
- If $-2 \le x \le 1$: the sum is $(1 - x) + (x + 2) = 3 < 5$, always true. This gives $[-2, 1]$.
- If $x > 1$: the sum is $2x + 1 < 5$, so $x < 2$. This gives $(1, 2)$.

Together: $(-3, 2)$. Geometrically, $|x - 1| + |x + 2|$ is the total distance from $x$ to the points $1$ and $-2$. It equals 3 anywhere between them and grows by 2 for each unit you move outside, reaching 5 at $x = 2$ and $x = -3$.

blocks.title: A square root
blocks.solution:
Domain: $x \ge -3$.

Case $x + 1 < 0$, that is $-3 \le x < -1$: the left side is at least 0 and the right side is negative, so the inequality holds. All of $[-3, -1)$ works.

Case $x + 1 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge -1$: both sides are non-negative, so squaring is allowed and gives an equivalent inequality: $x + 3 > x^2 + 2x + 1$, so $x^2 + x - 2 < 0$, so $(x + 2)(x - 1) < 0$, so $-2 < x < 1$. Combined with $x \ge -1$: $[-1, 1)$.

Solution: $[-3, 1)$. Check: at $x = 0$, $\sqrt3 > 1$; at $x = 1$, $2 > 2$ is false; at $x = 2$, $\sqrt5 > 3$ is false. Squaring without the case split would have produced $(-2, 1)$ and missed $[-3, -2]$.

blocks.title: Positive for every x
blocks.body: For which real $m$ is $x^2 - mx + m + 3 > 0$ for all real $x$?
blocks.solution:
The leading coefficient is $1 > 0$, so by the sign theorem the quadratic is positive for every $x$ exactly when it has no real root, that is when $\Delta < 0$. (If $\Delta = 0$ it equals 0 at the repeated root, and if $\Delta > 0$ it is negative between the roots.)

$$\Delta = m^2 - 4(m + 3) = m^2 - 4m - 12 = (m - 6)(m + 2) < 0 \iff -2 < m < 6.$$

Check the boundary $m = 6$: the quadratic is $x^2 - 6x + 9 = (x - 3)^2$, which is 0 at $x = 3$, so $m = 6$ is correctly excluded. An inequality about $x$ for all $x$ became an inequality about the parameter $m$.

blocks.title: Further: inequalities in two variables
blocks.body:
In the plane, a linear inequality $ax + by \le c$ (with $a, b$ not both 0) describes a half-plane: the line $ax + by = c$ and everything on one side of it. Test a point not on the line, such as the origin, to see which side. A system of several linear inequalities describes the intersection of half-planes, a convex polygonal region (possibly empty or unbounded).

For example $x \ge 0$, $y \ge 0$, $x + y \le 4$, $x + 2y \le 6$ is the quadrilateral with corners $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(2, 2)$ and $(0, 3)$; the corner $(2, 2)$ is where the two slanted lines cross. To maximise $3x + 4y$ over this region, notice that the lines $3x + 4y = k$ are parallel, and the largest $k$ whose line still meets the region touches it at a corner. Evaluating at the corners gives $0, 12, 14, 12$, so the maximum is 14 at $(2, 2)$. This "check the corners" principle is the start of [[linear-programming]].

For a university reader: the rules at the top of the page follow from the axioms of an ordered field (see [[real-numbers]]), so they hold in $\mathbb{Q}$ as well as $\mathbb{R}$; the sign-chart method additionally uses that a polynomial can only change sign at a root, which over $\mathbb{R}$ is a consequence of factorisation or of the intermediate value theorem (see [[continuity]]).

- Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality; multiplying by an expression of unknown sign is not allowed without splitting into cases.
- Do not "cancel" a common factor: $x^2 > x$ does not mean $x > 1$; it means $x(x - 1) > 0$, so $x < 0$ or $x > 1$.
- Squaring both sides is safe only when both sides are non-negative.
- The solution of $x^2 < 9$ is $-3 < x < 3$, not $x < \pm 3$.
- Zeros of a denominator are never part of the solution, even for $\le$ or $\ge$.
- Taking reciprocals reverses an inequality only when both sides have the same sign: $-1 < 2$ but $-1 < \frac12$.

Systems of linear inequalities lead to [[linear-programming]] and, more generally, [[convex-optimisation]]. Proving that an inequality holds for all values, rather than solving it, is the subject of [[amgm]] and [[cauchy-schwarz]]. Absolute-value inequalities are the language of limits: the definition of a limit on [[limits]] asks you to solve $|x - a| < \delta$ so that $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$. Rational expressions and their sign charts reappear on [[rational-functions]].

1. Solve $3 - 2x \ge 5x - 11$ and $-1 \le \frac{3 - x}{2} < 4$.
2. Solve $x^3 - 4x^2 - 5x \le 0$ and $\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x + 3} > 0$.
3. Solve $|x + 2| \ge 2x - 1$.
4. Find all $k$ for which $kx^2 + 4x + k > 0$ for every real $x$ (do not forget $k = 0$).
